name: West Slope - East Arete (Original Route)
text: [overview] The peak's original 1932 line: a moderate class 2 scramble up the west slope from the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch, most often climbed today as one link in the multi-day Southern Picket enchainment/traverse;

[beta] Reached from the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch (approached via Crescent Creek Basin as part of a Southern Pickets traverse), the west slope of West Twin Needle is class 2 — noticeably easier than the surrounding technical terrain of the Southern Pickets.

[approach] Same general Southern Pickets approach as the South Route — via Goodell Creek, The Barrier, and Crescent Creek Basin — continuing to the notch/saddle between Himmelhorn and West Twin Needle rather than climbing directly from the basin.

[turnaround] As with any link in the Southern Picket traverse, set a turnaround based on the whole enchainment's schedule — descending the class 3 east arete or class 2 west slope after dark adds significant risk on this exposed terrain.
[pro_tips] Most parties link this line into a full Southern Picket enchainment rather than climbing West Twin Needle alone from this side.
[pro_tips] This class 2-3 stretch is a noted 'reprieve' from the sustained 5th-class climbing found elsewhere on the Southern Picket traverse
earlierWhy: why: Class 2 slope via Southern Pickets approach; no direct text on snow or glaciers.

text: [hazards] Early-season snowfield on the approach can be firm enough to need an axe;

[descent_text] Unrope, cross the snow-covered saddle about 50 ft wide, and zigzag up third- and fourth-class ground, avoiding snowfields, to the summit;

name: Dike route
text: [approach] Snow on the dike and the face can be scouted from there before committing.
[descent_text] Many parties do not go on to the summit at all: after the Dike Pinnacle they bail out by dropping into Garnet Canyon's south fork, or by heading north onto the Middle Teton Glacier.
[descent_text] The ground from the pinnacle to Ellingwood Col is convoluted and needs a rappel, and the col itself is a steep snow crossing of about 40 degrees that holds snow all year.
earlierWhy: why: Ellingwood Col is a steep snow crossing that holds snow all year.

name: West Face
text: [overview] P1: the lone significant break in the lower headwall leads, via a chimney of great cracks, to an overhang (snow and ice early in the year), then a crumbly low-angle slab to a slung block (5.6, 35m).
[approach] early in the season it is a tongue of snow and ice over a short overhang, later a chimney.
[descent_text] Then rappel to the snow or choss gully, downclimb it, and rappel to the base.
earlierWhy: why: Snow and ice noted for early in the year only. | secondReview: no/unsure: Absaroka peak with no glacier on its west face, snow described only as early season and in a descent gully.

name: North Side Lowlight Tour (path of least resistance)
text: [overview] 6-7: ledge, 4th/easy 5th, then easy snow/3rd.

[approach] The climb starts at the top of the Grandstand, reached as for the North Face Highlight Tour: the Valhalla Traverse from the Lower Saddle, up the Grandstand from the Teton Glacier, or from Mt.
[approach] The Valhalla Traverse is the standard and starts at the Lower Saddle, while the Teton Glacier approach tends to see rockfall.
earlierWhy: why: Standard approach is the Valhalla Traverse; glacier approach optional. | secondReview: unsure/yes: It begins atop the Grandstand, reached by the snowy Valhalla Traverse or by the Teton Glacier, and its own text lists easy snow on the route.

name: Stettner Couloir
text: [overview] A steep couloir between two ridges on the south side of the Grand Teton, giving a snow and ice route to the summit in early summer.
[overview] As the season advances the snow melts out and rock climbing appears in the upper couloir, ending with a short rock step onto the broad southeast face.
[hazards] Exposed to avalanches spilling from the adjacent Ford Couloir, which catches early sun and fresh snow in late spring.
[hazards] Difficulty is highly condition-dependent — can be a moderate WI2-3 snow climb one season and a 5.7 waterfall-ice rock climb another
[gear] Crampons are a must;
[gear] Two 60 m ropes are ideal, both for a full-length rappel retreat and for the common ski/glacier descent.
[gear] Gear needs shift by season — expect more snow/ice tools in spring/early summer, more rock rack in late summer and fall
[detailed_rack] On snow and ice: small cams (a couple) or screws (a couple).
[approach] or come from the east via the Teepe Glacier, Teepe Col and Glencoe Col, which is the more common approach.
[descent_text] Above the chockstone crux the couloir broadens to the narrow saddle between the Underhill Ridge and the summit snowfield.
[descent_text] Turn left, climb third-class slabs mixed with snow, and take the best line up the snowfield to the top.
earlierWhy: why: Snow and ice route in early summer; common approach crosses the Teepe Glacier.

name: Glencoe-Teepe Chute
text: [approach] A long snow slope leads to the base of the gully.
[approach] Steep snow slopes here are avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast.
[descent_text] From the col, the way down is the Teepe Glacier.
